title: The Story of the Weeping Camel
full_review:
In "The Story of the Weeping Camel" (ThinkFilm), a family of nomadic herders summons a musician from a far-off village to perform an ancient ritual in the hopes of coaxing a mother camel into nursing the newborn calf which she rejected at birth.

Set amid the sweeping vistas of the Gobi Desert, with a cast of nonprofessional actors, directors Byambasuren Davaa and Luigi Falorni have crafted a beautifully told tale whose message of family bonds, the importance of tradition and the centrality of love for survival is both heartbreaking and heartwarming.

Visually elegant and emotionally affecting, this modest gem of a movie has both the unadorned immediacy of a documentary and the contemplative poeticism of a fable. Reminiscent of Robert J. Flaherty's 1922 "Nanook of the North," the docudrama combines unrehearsed sequences with staged recreations to create a blend of documentary and fiction, resulting in a narrative-documentary hybrid.

The film opens in spring and follows the daily routine of a four-generation clan of sheep and camel herders (played by a family of real-life nomads), living on the windswept steppes of southern Mongolia, whose all-but-vanished way of life has remained relatively unspoiled by the encroachment of modernity -- though the film's final image shows it to be a losing battle.

After a particularly difficult labor, one of the camels in their fold gives birth to a snow-white colt. But the joy is short-lived as the camel quickly gives its offspring the cold hump, refusing to allow the colt to nurse. The herders realize that without its mother's milk the little camel will not survive. When their efforts to wheedle the mother into bonding with her child prove futile, the clan, in accordance with time-honored tradition, dispatches two of its youngest members to fetch a violinist who can perform an age-old musical rite which, according to legend, will jump-start the animal's maternal instinct. Legend also holds that, if the ceremony has been successful, the plaintive tune will make the mother camel cry -- thus justifying the title of the film.

Though it doesn't sound like much of a plot, "The Story of the Weeping Camel" is a cinematic oasis in a desert of blockbuster banality. Billed by the filmmakers as "equal parts reality, drama and magic" -- it delivers on all three counts.

The images of the baby camel crying for its mother's affection as it stumbles across the barren landscape are heartrending, especially when juxtaposed with shots of the other colts coddling contently with their own mothers -- the net result being, by the end of the film, the camel isn't the only one weeping.

And while the dysfunctional dromedaries (actually, they are two-humped Bactrian camels) are the true stars of the film, their human co-stars bring an honesty and unvarnished sincerity to their mostly improvised performances. This is especially true about the wizened patriarch (Janchiv Ayurzana) and his adorable great-grandson (Uuganbaatar Ikhbayar) whose contagious smile needs no translation.

Though the story takes place in an exotic locale, the thematic terrain explored -- that of the love between a mother and child -- couldn't be more universal. In fact, it was the universality of the film's underlying message which first attracted the filmmakers to the project. "It is the story of salvation," says Falorni. "The little starving camel is each of us, estranged, unceasingly searching for protection and needing to belong. The baby camel's fate is visible evidence that no life is possible without love."

While such sobering sentiments may be challenging to a world intoxicated by an inflated sense of hyper-individualism, they eloquently echo the Christian understanding of humanity's hunger for God's love, the divine sustenance upon which our continued existence depends. The film's central image of a suckling babe desperately seeking the succor of its mother's life-giving milk provides a beautiful visual for meditating on the words of Isaiah, where the prophet symbolically compares our intimate relationship with God to that of "a child that is nursed by its mother."

Subtitles.

Due to thematic content, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
